From photographs to a paper: the intraitR apps, step by step

Source: vignettes/apps-workflow.Rmd
apps-workflow.Rmd

Version française : vignette("apps-workflow-fr", package = "intraitR").

What intraitR is for

intraitR measures the morphology of fishes on photographs and analyses it, from the first click to a reproducible project ready for a paper. It follows the FISHMORPH protocol (Brosse et al. 2021): landmarks placed on a lateral photograph give eleven linear measurements and the nine unitless ratios that describe locomotion and food acquisition (Villéger et al. 2010). Because each specimen is measured individually, intraitR is built for intraspecific trait variability (ITV): how much individuals of one species differ, compared with how much species differ.

Everything can be done from R, but the usual path goes through four applications that open in the browser, one after the other:

Step Application Opened by What you do there
1 Start page launch_measure_hub() without arguments choose (or upload) the photographs, the species, where results are saved
2 Measurement hub the start page, or launch_measure_hub(photo_dir, ...) select photographs, run the automatic pre-pass, follow progress, check results
3 Digitizer the hub (3. Digitize) place, predict and correct the landmarks, photograph by photograph
4 Analyses the hub (4. Results), or launch_intrait_analyses() traits, trait space, FISHMORPH, ITV, shape, measurement error; export a reproducible project

Two companion packages plug into the same hub: Rfishmorph (the FISHMORPH reference database and its functional space) and, for a campaign database, FishInTrait (see the last section).

Before the first session 

install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("FunTraits/Rfishmorph")
remotes::install_github("FunTraits/intraitR")

# Once per computer, optional: the models that predict the landmarks
# (~290 MB, downloaded from the GitHub release of intraitR) and their
# Python environment. Without them every point is placed by hand.
intraitR::install_mlmorph_models()
intraitR::install_mlmorph_python()

The start page shows whether the models are installed, and offers the same two installations with a button.

Photographs. One fish (or several, see plates) per photograph, lateral view, head to the left if possible, with a scale bar of known length in the plane of the fish. The file name without its extension becomes the specimen code. Organise the folder in two levels if you can — for example site/date/photo.jpg — the hub uses them as folder and sub-folder.

Step 1 — the start page 

library(intraitR)
res <- launch_measure_hub()
  1. Photographs. Browse to the folder (the number of photographs in each sub-folder is shown), or upload photographs into a new folder. An upload never copies a photograph that is already there under another name, nor the same file twice: a window lists them.
  2. Species. Not known yet; one folder per species (the folder names are the species); or from a table (CSV or Excel: one row per photograph, a column naming the photograph and a column species, optionally source for the provenance — campaign, museum…).
  3. Where to save. The workbook (.xlsx) and the journal folder. Defaults are next to the photographs. The journal is the source of truth: every saved specimen is appended to it at once and never rewritten; the workbook is an export that can always be rebuilt from it (consolidate_landmarks()).
  4. Session. Operator (traced in every record), length of the scale bar.
  5. Open the photographs. The bottom of the page shows the equivalent console call, to start the same session from a script next time; the last sessions are listed and can be reopened in one click.

Step 2 — the measurement hub

The hub keeps running during the whole session; the other applications open in their own browser tabs and the hub follows what they write.

Home. Progress of the folder (measured / to measure, per folder), the last saves, Resume where you stopped, and the other applications.

1. Setup. Operator, scale-bar length, where the predictor lives; the applications currently open (and Close them all).

2. Select. Choose a folder, then a sub-folder: the gallery shows every photograph with its species and its state (measured or not). Click to select; Select shown not measured takes everything left to do. The magnifier opens a photograph in large. Next: digitize the selection →.

3. Digitize.

  • Automatic pre-pass (optional): batch_landmarks() predicts the points of the whole selection in the background, hinges 22/24 included (useful for curved fish). The predictions arrive in the digitizer as predicted points, to be checked.
  • Open the digitizer on exactly the selection (step 3 below).
  • Accept the pre-pass without review records the predictions as they are, after a warning: use it only for photographs you will not check, and know that they stay marked predicted / not reviewed in the journal.

4. Results. The menus at the top choose what the tables, the traits and the analyses are computed on — empty means everything:

Menu Selects
Folder, Sub-folder photographs (e.g. sites, dates)
Species photographs and literature records
Provenance campaign, museum… and literature (trait records without photographs, when the hub has them)
Studies the published data sets, when literature is chosen

A line summarises the selection (photographs, measured, species, literature records). Tabs:

  • Progress: measured / to measure per folder, sub-folder and species.
  • Landmarks & statuses: for each specimen, how its points were obtained — clicked/validated (checked by the operator), adjusted (moved by a protocol convention), predicted (model, not reviewed), seeded (never moved: not measured), derived, na — and how many expected points are missing.
  • Traits: Compute the FISHMORPH traits — the eleven measurements (cm, or pixels for a photograph without a scale bar: its ratios remain exact) and the nine ratios, plus the literature records chosen.
  • Annotated photograph: the points drawn on the photograph; Correct the points in the digitizer reopens this photograph alone, in correct mode.

💾 Save to the database re-reads everything and registers the measurements (with FishInTrait: in the project manifest). Finish closes the digitizer and the hub and returns to R.

Step 3 — the digitizer

One photograph at a time. The landmark buttons on the right say which point the next click places; numbering follows FISHMORPH: 1 snout, 2 caudal fin base, 3–19 the anatomical points, 20–21 the two ends of the scale bar, 22, 24, 25 hinges along the body midline of a curved fish (standard length is then measured along the bent line), 23 the head base (derived).

Action How
Place a point click on the photograph
Predict the 19 anatomical points click 1 (snout) and 2 (caudal fin base), then Predict 19 landmarks; the scale bar is predicted too if not placed (status predicted until clicked)
Predict without clicking Auto (no clicks) (needs the global model)
Undo / redo Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Shift+Z (Cmd on a Mac), or the buttons
Validate the points Validate points
Save and go to the next photograph Enter, or Save & next
A point that cannot be seen Mark NA
Zoom, pan Zoom + / −, Whole view, the arrows
Write the workbook now 💾 Write the workbook now (it is also written regularly)

Three queues, from the action bar: new (photographs not yet measured), correct (measured specimens, points reloaded, to move the wrong ones) and repeat (the same photograph measured several times, blind by default: these passes go to the bias sheet and give the measurement error). Several fish on one photograph: + individual (the codes become <photo>_i1, _i2… and share the scale bar).

Before saving, protocol checks run: eye vertical, extreme points 3/4, the coincidence rules of FISHMORPH. A suspicious specimen is shown with Measure again, Auto-correct and save or Save without correcting.

Finish writes the workbook and closes the digitizer; the hub notices and refreshes.

Step 4 — the analyses, and a project ready for a paper

In 4. Results, set the menus, then 📊 Analyses → reproducible project (.zip). The analyses application opens on the measured photographs (and the literature records) of the selection. It also runs on its own:

launch_intrait_analyses(xlsx_path = "landmarks.xlsx")
Tab Content Functions
1. Data sample per species (Table 1); minimum number of individuals per species, species, sites, provenance; ratios used (with the share of records that have each ratio, per provenance and study); landmark corrections fishmorph_segments(), fishmorph_ratios()
2. Traits the ratios per species, coefficients of variation summary_traits(), intraspecific_variability()
3. Trait space PCA of the log-transformed, standardised ratios; dispersion per species, permutation tests (Holm) trait_space(), trait_disparity()
4. FISHMORPH the sample in the space of ~9,000 freshwater species; share of the global space project_fishmorph()
5. ITV variance between vs within species (and between sites); rarefaction and the number of individuals needed (n*) itv_index(), itv_accumulation()
6. Shape Procrustes superimposition, shape space, shape disparity gpa_fish(), shape_space()
7. Measurement error %ME and repeatability per measurement, placement error per landmark (repeat passes) measurement_error(), digitization_error()
8. Export the project (.zip) and its report write_analysis_project()

Export. Give a title, the authors and a folder name, then Build the project. The project has the architecture of a published paper:

my_project/
├── scripts/      00_START, 01_DATA, 02_ANALYSIS, 03_FIGURE_*, 04_SUPP_*, 05_STAT_*
├── utils/        library.R, parameters.R (every parameter, one place), functions.R
├── data/         raw/ (landmarks as digitized, literature records), processed/, metadata.csv
├── results/      figures/ (Fig*, FigS*: png + pdf), tables/ (Table*, TableS*: csv)
├── manuscript/   Methods_Results.Rmd and .docx, references.bib
├── run_all.R     runs everything, then renders the report
└── README.md, <project>.Rproj, .gitignore, session_info.txt

The tables, figures and report are not copies of the screen: the export runs the project’s own scripts (run_all.R, in a separate R session), so the archive contains exactly what anyone obtains by running it again. Change a value in utils/parameters.R and re-run run_all.R to update everything.

The report (manuscript/Methods_Results.docx) contains the Methods and the Results only, with every number read from results/tables/ and the references. Text in [square brackets] is for you to complete (sampling, photographic protocol, data sets used) — the application cannot know it.

Other applications of the hub

The Apps menu opens, in their own tabs: the FISHMORPH functional space (Rfishmorph) and, when the hub is started by FishInTrait, the applications of the campaign database.

With FishInTrait (campaign database)

FishInTrait manages a sampling campaign: photographs received from the field, specimen codes, sites, dates, identifications, published data sets. It opens the same hub on its project:

library(FishInTrait)
p <- fit_project_open("path/to/00_project")
launch_fishintrait_measure(p, operator = "AT")
Need Application (from the hub’s Apps menu or a photograph)
Bring in photographs, a field sheet, landmarks Import — launch_fishintrait_import(): project, delivery (with a check of the photographs already imported), field sheet, photographs (species, count, pose), import, corrections, quality & export
Add published trait data Literature — launch_fishintrait_literature()
Crop, turn, re-identify one photograph Edit this photograph — launch_fishintrait_photo()
Check identifications Review — launch_fishintrait_review()
Explore traits by site, species, in the FISHMORPH space Explore — launch_fishintrait_explorer()

The hub then knows the provenance of every photograph (campaign or museum) and offers the project’s literature in 4. Results. Published records have no photograph: they enter the traits and every analysis based on the ratios, never the landmark tables, the shape or the measurement error. A data set may lack a ratio (for instance one without PFv): the Data tab of the analyses shows it, and unchecking that ratio brings its records in — say so, and why, in the Methods.

Without the applications

Every step has its function, to script or to reproduce a session:

q   <- measure_queue("photos", species = "folder", journal_dir = "journal")
batch_landmarks(...)                          # automatic pre-pass
digitize_landmarks(photo_dir = "photos", xlsx_path = "landmarks.xlsx",
                   journal_dir = "journal", operator = "AT")
consolidate_landmarks("journal", xlsx_path = "landmarks.xlsx")  # workbook rebuilt from the journal
fish <- read_digitizer_workbook("landmarks.xlsx")  # every point, hinges 24/25 included
seg <- fishmorph_segments(fish, scale_cm = 1)
rat <- fishmorph_ratios(seg)
write_analysis_project(fish, "my_project", params = analysis_params(min_n = 10))

When something goes wrong

Symptom Cause, remedy
Predict says no model is available install_mlmorph_models() then install_mlmorph_python(), once per computer
A specimen measured before reappears as new it was saved in another workbook or journal: always give the same xlsx_path, journal_dir and operator
Measurement error: “every individual must have at least 2 replicates” (older versions) a photograph of the bias sheet was digitized once; it is now left out and named — digitize it a second time
Literature records never analysed a ratio is missing from the data set: see the coverage table of 1. Data
Bl and BEl seem too low on curved fish place the hinges 22/24(/25) on the midline; standard length then follows the body
A workbook looks wrong rebuild it from the journal: Rebuild from the journal in the digitizer, or consolidate_landmarks()

References

Brosse S, Charpin N, Su G, Toussaint A, Herrera-R GA, Tedesco PA, Villéger S (2021) FISHMORPH: a global database on morphological traits of freshwater fishes. Global Ecology and Biogeography 30: 2330–2336.

Villéger S, Ramos Miranda J, Flores Hernández D, Mouillot D (2010) Contrasting changes in taxonomic vs. functional diversity of tropical fish communities after habitat degradation. Ecological Applications 20: 1512–1522.

Violle C, Enquist BJ, McGill BJ, Jiang L, Albert CH, Hulshof C, Jung V, Messier J (2012) The return of the variance: intraspecific variability in community ecology. Trends in Ecology & Evolution 27: 244–252.
